notes: Use v = fλ and f = 1/T. A spatial separation between equal-phase points gives wavelength; a time separation gives period.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w1:a.hint: Check whether the question compares amplitude, intensity, or total power; these do not scale in the same way.
notes: For the same medium and frequency, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared. For an isotropic point source, I = P/(4πr²).
When coherent waves overlap, add their signed displacements first and then square the resultant amplitude. Adding intensities alone loses the interference effect.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w1:b.hint: Compare the particle’s displacement direction with the direction in which the wave travels.
notes: Transverse waves have particle oscillations perpendicular to propagation; longitudinal waves have them parallel. Energy travels even though particles oscillate locally.
For a moving wave profile, use a slightly later snapshot to infer the particle’s next displacement. Do not assume a particle moves along the plotted curve.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w1:c.hint: Use the initial displacement and initial direction of motion to decide where the oscillation starts.
notes: For x = A cos(ωt + φ), v = −ωA sin(ωt + φ) and a = −ω²x. Velocity is a quarter-cycle out of phase with displacement.
Read amplitude from the equilibrium line and period between equivalent points. A zero crossing alone does not identify whether the motion is upwards or downwards.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w2:b.hint: Compare the driving frequency with the system’s natural frequency, then consider the damping.
notes: Resonance is a large forced response when the driving frequency is near a natural frequency. Energy must be supplied by the driver.
More damping reduces the peak response and broadens the resonance. Distinguish driving frequency from the free oscillation that would occur without the driver.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w2:c.hint: Mark the boundary conditions at both ends, then fit the simplest allowed pattern between them.
notes: Fixed string ends and closed pipe ends are displacement nodes; an open pipe end is a displacement antinode. Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart; a node and adjacent antinode are λ/4 apart.
Two like ends allow L = nλ/2. One open and one closed end allows L = (2n − 1)λ/4. Use the mode shown, not automatically the fundamental.

Wave speed is the speed of a disturbance, not the speed of one oscillating particle. Keep the wave’s travel direction separate from the direction of particle motion.

ibd-f8bc226e91319945-q12:whole.hint: Check whether the question compares amplitude, intensity, or total power; these do not scale in the same way.
notes: For the same medium and frequency, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared. For an isotropic point source, I = P/(4πr²).
When coherent waves overlap, add their signed displacements first and then square the resultant amplitude. Adding intensities alone loses the interference effect.

duplicate-57d14bc616568e0e.hint: Compare the particle’s displacement direction with the direction in which the wave travels.
notes: Transverse waves have particle oscillations perpendicular to propagation; longitudinal waves have them parallel. Energy travels even though particles oscillate locally.
For a moving wave profile, use a slightly later snapshot to infer the particle’s next displacement. Do not assume a particle moves along the plotted curve.
